description_full: The Buckle, Inc. operates as a retailer of casual apparel, footwear, and accessories for men, women, and kids under the Buckle and Buckle Youth brands in the United States. The company markets a selection of brand name casual apparel, including denims, other casual bottoms, tops, sportswear, outerwear, accessories, and footwear, as well as private label merchandise comprising the BKE, Buckle Black, Ace High, Daytrip, Departwest, FITZ + EDDI, Freshwear, Gentry Country, Gilded Intent, Gimmicks, J.B. Holt, Maven Co-op, Modish Rebel, Nova Industries, Outpost Makers, Reclaim, Salvage, Sterling & Stitch, Veece, Willow & Root, 33 Coastal, and Funk Lagoon brands. It also provides services, such as hemming, gift-packaging, layaways, a guest loyalty program, the Buckle private label credit card, personalized stylist services, and a special-order system that allows stores to obtain specifically requested merchandise from other company stores or from its online order fulfillment center. The company was formerly known as Mills Clothing, Inc. and changed its name to The Buckle, Inc. in April 1991. The Buckle, Inc. was incorporated in 1948 and is headquartered in Kearney, Nebraska.

financial_summary: Buckle, Inc. (The) is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $2.2B market cap on $1.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 52% against a 9% cost of capital — a 43-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 44%.

The business throws off $206M in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.20× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.0× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 10.4% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 38% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.4× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 13pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.44x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-5.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 17% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 28% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 31% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market.
About $18.5M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 53% in the 2020 crash, 35% in the 2022 bear market and 62% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 26% below its DCF fair value of $56.54, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 28%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $46.05 to $70.52 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 9.7 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 7.8 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 10.5 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 72% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 9.5% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 11.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $46.00 on average, 10% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 52% clears the cost of capital of 9.3% by 43pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.29).
It runs a 44% gross margin and converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.20x.
ROE of 49% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $287.2M (13% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.0, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -1.2% over 3 years, 7.6% over 5 years and 1.5% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 12%).
At current returns, reinvesting 3% of profits supports about 1.5% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -1.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 1.8x depreciation (3.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 9.6% on average.
Analysts expect -3.5% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 38.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 63%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $7.1M sold).
It returns 10.4% a year to shareholders (3.3% in dividends).
The share count has grown 0.7% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It has paid a dividend for 23 consecutive years, raising it 11.9% a year over the last five.
Short interest is elevated at 11.9% of the float, 7.9 days to cover.
people: With about 2,900 employees, each generates about $448K of revenue, 1.2x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 2.1% a year.
That works out to $71K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $6.0M (13x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
